title: The Cases
summary: Telugu marks the work a noun does by gluing a suffix onto it. The suffixes are few and regular; the stem they are glued to is what varies, and that stem — the oblique — is a case in its own right, the genitive.

rules.heading: Suffixes Are Glued, Not Fused
rules.statement: Telugu is an **agglutinative** language: it marks grammar by adding suffixes that keep their own shape and can be peeled off again. A Lithuanian ending fuses case and number into one syllable that cannot be divided; a Telugu suffix is a separate piece added to a stem that is still recognisable. The same suffix serves every noun in the language.
footnotes: The suffixes stack: a plural ending and then a case suffix after it, which a fused declension cannot do (¶63).

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985, §9.12.
sources.note: Case suffixes as postpositions added to nouns.

rules.heading: The Seven Cases
rules.statement: Telugu marks seven cases: nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, instrumental, locative and vocative. Only four of them are a suffix glued to a stem — the nominative adds nothing, the genitive is the bare oblique stem (¶60), and the vocative is a change in the noun's own last vowel (¶70).

paradigms.caption: Four nouns declined in the singular
paradigms.footnote: A dash marks a case the noun is not used in: a book is not called to, and a person is not a place. The four columns are four different oblique classes (¶61), which is where the forms differ; the suffixes on the right of them are the same throughout.

paradigms.caption: The same four in the plural
paradigms.footnote: The plural has one oblique for every class, in **-ల** (¶63), so the six classes of the singular collapse to one here.

sources.citation: Brown, Charles Philip, *A Grammar of the Telugu Language*, 2nd ed. Madras: Christian Knowledge Society's Press, 1857, the chapter "On Nouns", on the cases and the declensions.
sources.note: "Accordingly the cases found in Telugu are the Nominative, Genitive, Dative, Accusative, Vocative, Instrumental and Locative."

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985, §8.5, §8.9, §9.8–9.9.
sources.note: Source for the oblique stems and the suffixed forms.

rules.heading: The Nominative
rules.statement: The nominative is the bare noun, carrying no suffix at all, and it is the form a dictionary cites. A subject stands in it, and so, very often, does an inanimate object (¶64).

examples.note: both నేను and పుస్తకం stand bare

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985, §9.7.
sources.note: The unsuffixed form used as the accusative of inanimates.

rules.heading: The Oblique Stem Is the Genitive
rules.statement: Beside its nominative every noun has an **oblique stem**, and that stem standing alone is the genitive: **రాముడి కలం**, *Rama's pen*. Every suffix of the other cases is added to it, so the oblique is at once a case of its own and the base the rest are built on.

paradigms.caption: Nominative and oblique
paradigms.footnote: **అమ్మ** shows an oblique identical with its nominative, which is the commonest case of all (¶61, class A).

footnotes: The written language also has **యొక్క** for the genitive: **అతని యొక్క పేరు** beside **అతని పేరు**, both *his name*.

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985, §8.2, §8.10.
sources.note: "every noun has an oblique stem in the singular that is sometimes called the 'possessive form' … It corresponds in meaning to the possessive (genitive) singular form ending in 's in English."

sources.citation: Brown, Charles Philip, *A Grammar of the Telugu Language*, 2nd ed. Madras: Christian Knowledge Society's Press, 1857, the chapter "On Nouns".
sources.note: "The Genitive case, if it differs from the nominative is often called the inflection"; and "The Genitive often uses యొక్క 'of'."

rules.heading: The Six Classes of Oblique Stem
rules.statement: Nouns fall into six classes by the way the oblique is formed. In the largest it is identical with the nominative; the others add **-ి**, or replace the last syllable with **-టి** or **-తి**, or take a separate form before two of the cases.

paradigms.caption: The six classes

rows.label: A
cells: unchanged — stems in -అ, -ఎ, a long vowel, or a doubled consonant

rows.label: C
cells: final syllable → -టి — non-human nouns of two or more syllables

rows.label: E
cells: final syllable → -తి — five stems in -యి and two in -ర్రు

paradigms.footnote: Class D is closed at six stems and class E at seven. Class A holds the majority of Telugu nouns, and words taken from other languages join it: **రోడ్డు** and **ఫోన్** change nothing.

examples.gloss: house → of a house → to the house
hand → of a hand → in the hand
tree → of a tree → to the tree

footnotes: Some class B and C stems survive only inside a compound: **చంటి బిడ్డ**, *infant*, keeps the oblique of **చన్ను**, and **నాగటి కోల**, *plough-shaft*, that of **నాగలి**, while the free dative is **నాగలికి**.
Several class B and C nouns are moving into class A: **కాలుకు** beside **కాలికి**, *to a leg*.

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985, §8.5, §8.6–8.7.
sources.note: The six classes A–F, their membership, the frozen compounds, and the drift of classes B and C into class A.

rules.heading: A Noun in -ం Has Two Obliques
rules.statement: A noun ending in **-ం** takes the nominative unchanged as its genitive, and a second oblique in **-ాని-** before the accusative and the dative. **పుస్తకం** is *of a book*, but *to a book* is **పుస్తకానికి**.

paradigms.caption: The two obliques
paradigms.footnote: The instrumental and the locative are built on the genitive oblique, not on the second one: **పుస్తకంతో**, **పుస్తకంలో**.

footnotes: A stem in **-ెం** takes **-ేని-** instead: **పళ్ళెం**, *plate*, gives **పళ్ళేనికి**.

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985, §8.5F, §9.9.
sources.note: "All nouns ending in [am/em] have two oblique stems each, one in the genitive without any modification and another before the accusative and dative case suffixes."

rules.heading: The Oblique in the Plural
rules.statement: The plural forms its oblique by changing **-లు** to **-ల** and **-ళ్ళు** to **-ళ్ళ**. Case suffixes are added to that, so the plural marker and the case stand one after the other, each keeping its own shape.

paradigms.caption: Plural, oblique, and two cases
paradigms.footnote: The six singular classes of ¶61 leave no trace here: whatever a noun does in the singular, its plural oblique ends in **-ల** or **-ళ్ళ**.

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985, §8.9.
sources.note: The plural oblique in -ల / -ళ.

rules.heading: The Accusative — ని / ను
rules.statement: The direct object takes **-ని** or **-ను**. A noun naming an animate being takes it necessarily; with a lifeless thing it is optional, and the bare nominative is the commoner choice.

examples.note: inanimate, so the noun is bare

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985, §9.4, §9.7.
sources.note: "nouns denoting animate objects must take the accusative suffix, whereas with inanimate nouns its use is optional."

rules.heading: The Dative — కి / కు
rules.statement: **-కి** or **-కు** marks the person to whom or for whom, and it is the busiest suffix in the language. Beside the indirect object it does work that English gives to a subject: with it Telugu says that a thing is liked, is needed, or is *had*.

paradigms.caption: The dative of the pronouns
paradigms.footnote: Which of the two shapes appears is settled by ¶66.

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985, §9.2, §9.12.
sources.note: The dative postposition and the range of its uses.

rules.heading: When It Is -ని and -కి, and When -ను and -కు
rules.statement: Both pairs choose by the sound in front of them: **-ని** and **-కి** follow a stem whose last syllable ends in **ఇ** or **ఈ**, and **-ను** and **-కు** follow every other. The personal pronouns with a one-syllable oblique are the exception — **నీకు** and **మీకు**, not నీకి.

paradigms.caption: The two shapes
paradigms.footnote: **నీ** and **మీ** end in ఈ and still take **-కు**; they are the exception the rule names.

footnotes: Modern Standard Telugu extends **-ని** and **-కి** past that condition: **అన్నని** and **అన్నకి** alternate freely with **అన్నను** and **అన్నకు**.

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985, §9.5.
sources.note: "The postpositions [nu] and [ku] take the forms [ni] and [ki] if the preceding syllable ends in [i] or [ii], except in the case of personal pronouns with monosyllabic oblique stems"; and the note on the Modern Standard drift.

sources.citation: Brown, Charles Philip, *A Grammar of the Telugu Language*, 2nd ed. Madras: Christian Knowledge Society's Press, 1857, the chapter "On Nouns".
sources.note: "The Dative … adds కి to the inflection if it ends in ఇ or ఈ … But if the inflection ends in any other syllable it takes కు."

rules.heading: The Instrumental — తో
rules.statement: **-తో** covers both what English divides between *with* the instrument and *with* the companion: *written with a pen* and *came with a friend* take the same suffix. The written language also has **-చేత**, which marks the instrument and the agent but not the companion.
footnotes: A bare **-న** on the oblique serves as an instrumental in the older language: **కర్రన కొట్టాడు**, *he struck with a stick*.

sources.citation: Brown, Charles Philip, *A Grammar of the Telugu Language*, 2nd ed. Madras: Christian Knowledge Society's Press, 1857, the chapter "On Nouns".
sources.note: "The instrumental case adds to the inflection the words చేత 'by' or తో 'with'"; and the note on న used for the instrumental.

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985, §9.14.
sources.note: తో listed among the bound postpositions.

rules.heading: The Locative — లో, మీద
rules.statement: **-లో** means *in* and **-మీద** means *on*, and neither is a preposition: nothing in Telugu stands before its noun as English *in* and *on* do. The older written language marks the same case with **-అందు** or a bare **-న**.
footnotes: **ఇంటిలో** contracts to **ఇంట్లో** in speech and in writing alike.
**లో** and **మీద** are postpositions of the second type (¶71), so a further suffix goes on top of them: **ఇంట్లోకి**, *into the house*.

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985, §9.14–9.15.
sources.note: లో and మీద as independent-word postpositions, and లోకి, లోనుంచి.

sources.citation: Brown, Charles Philip, *A Grammar of the Telugu Language*, 2nd ed. Madras: Christian Knowledge Society's Press, 1857, the chapter "On Nouns".
sources.note: "the Locative case adds అందు or లో 'in'."

rules.heading: The Ablative — నుండి
rules.statement: **-నుండి** — or **-నుంచి**, which is commoner in speech — means *from*, of place and of time alike. It is added to the oblique stem like the rest: **ఇంటి నుండి**, *from the house*.
footnotes: Telugu's own grammars give the ablative no case of its own, reckoning it with the instrumental or the locative (¶72).

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985, §9.13–9.14.
sources.note: నుంచి / నించి among the bound postpositions.

rules.heading: The Vocative
rules.statement: A noun is called by lengthening its final vowel: **అక్క** gives **అక్కా**, **తండ్రి** gives **తండ్రీ**. A noun in **-డు** may take **-డా** instead, and a noun in **-ం** has no vocative at all.

paradigms.caption: Calling and naming
paradigms.footnote: The vocative is the one case that adds no suffix: the noun's own last vowel is lengthened and nothing is glued on.

examples.note: an affectionate address, used even to a small girl

footnotes: The plural vocative in **-లారా** — **అక్కలారా**, *O sisters* — belongs to platform speech and to writing.
Relatives address each other by the kinship term rather than by name: **బావా**, **వదినా**, **తమ్ముడూ**.

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985, §25.5.
sources.note: "In calling or addressing a person the last vowel of the word or name by which the person is called is lengthened; if the last syllable is [Du], it may occasionally be changed to [Daa]. Words/names ending in [am] do not take a vocative suffix."

sources.citation: Brown, Charles Philip, *A Grammar of the Telugu Language*, 2nd ed. Madras: Christian Knowledge Society's Press, 1857, the section "On the Vocative".
sources.note: "All nouns ending in ఇ make the singular vocative by lengthening the final vowel"; and the plural in -లారా.

rules.heading: The Case Suffixes Are Postpositions
rules.statement: What is called a case suffix here is a **postposition**: a piece that follows the oblique stem where English would put a preposition in front. Some are bound and never stand alone — **-ని**, **-కి**, **-తో**, **-నుంచి**; others are separate words, and a bound one may then be added on top of them.

paradigms.caption: The two types

rows.label: bound
cells: never a word on its own; nothing may follow

rows.label: free
cells: also ordinary nouns of place; take a bound suffix after them
లో, మీద, కింద, లోపల, ముందు, వెనుక

paradigms.footnote: **లో** *in* gives **లోకి** *into* and **లోనుంచి** *from inside*, each a bound suffix added to a free one.

examples.gloss: The car is on the road.

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985, §9.12, §9.14–9.15.
sources.note: The division into Type 1 (bound) and Type 2 (independent words), with లో, లోనుంచి and లోకి as the illustration.

rules.heading: What the Telugu Grammarians Count
rules.statement: Telugu's own grammars count the cases on the Sanskrit model and name them by number — **ప్రథమా విభక్తి**, the first case, and so on. That scheme does not cut where the European one does: the genitive and the dative fall together under **షష్ఠీ**, the sixth.

paradigms.caption: The two namings
paradigms.footnote: Brown, who sets out these equivalences, prefers the European arrangement and writes that Telugu grammarians "have made fruitless efforts to mould the noun on the Sanscrit model".

footnotes: **ఏకవచనము** is the singular and **బహువచనము** the plural in the same tradition.

sources.citation: Brown, Charles Philip, *A Grammar of the Telugu Language*, 2nd ed. Madras: Christian Knowledge Society's Press, 1857, the chapter "On Nouns", footnote on the Sanskrit case names.
sources.note: "Sanscrit grammarians (from whom Telugu authors borrow their rules) call the nominative ప్రథమావిభక్తి First case; the Accusative ద్వితీయావిభక్తి Second case; the Instrumental తృతీయావిభక్తి Third case; the Genitive and Dative are included in షష్ఠి the Sixth case; and the Locative is called సప్తమివిభక్తి the Seventh case. The Ablative is called either తృతీయ Instrumental or సప్తమి Locative."

drills.stem: How is **to me** said?
drills.explanation: The oblique stem of నేను is నా-, and the dative suffix is added to that: *నాకు*. Adding -కు to the nominative gives a form that does not exist.

drills.stem: Which suffix means **from**?
drills.explanation: -నుండి, or -నుంచి in speech. -మీద means *on* and -ని marks a direct object.

drills.stem: Telugu has no separate word for **Rama's**. What carries that sense?
options: The oblique stem standing alone, రాముడి.
drills.explanation: The oblique stem is the genitive: *రాముడి కలం*, Rama's pen. It is the one case that is a stem rather than a suffix, and it is also the base every other suffix is added to.

drills.stem: What does it mean to say that Telugu is **agglutinative**?
options: That its words are very long.
That grammatical suffixes keep their own shape and can be separated from the stem.
That its endings fuse case and number into one syllable.
drills.explanation: The last option describes a fusional language such as Lithuanian, where one ending carries case and number together and cannot be divided. A Telugu suffix is a separate piece, the same on every noun.

drills.stem: Why is there no word standing **before** the noun in *పుస్తకంలో* (in the book)?
options: Because the word for *in* has been left out.
Because Telugu puts after the noun what English puts before it.
Because పుస్తకం is a special noun.
Because the phrase is in the plural.
drills.explanation: -లో is a postposition, not a preposition. Telugu has postpositions and suffixes and no prepositions at all — the head follows what depends on it throughout the language.

drills.stem: *to a book* is **పుస్తకానికి**, but *of a book* is simply **పుస్తకం**. Why?
options: Because the genitive has been left unmarked by accident.
Because a noun in -ం has two obliques: the bare nominative for the genitive, and -ాని- before the accusative and the dative.
Because the dative is irregular for this noun.
drills.explanation: Class F is the only class with two oblique stems. The dative suffix -కి is perfectly regular; it is the stem in front of it that is chosen differently from the one the genitive uses.

drills.stem: *నేను పుస్తకం చదువుతున్నాను* has no suffix on **పుస్తకం**, though it is the object. Why not?
options: Because the sentence is in the present.
Because the object is inanimate, and with an inanimate object the accusative suffix is optional.
Because పుస్తకం cannot take a suffix.
Because the suffix has been dropped in error.
drills.explanation: An animate object must carry -ని or -ను; an inanimate one need not, and usually does not. The bare form is the more idiomatic of the two.

drills.stem: How would you say **with a friend**?
drills.explanation: -తో covers both the instrument and the companion — *with a pen* and *with a friend* alike. The others give *to*, *in* and *from*.

drills.stem: **అమ్మ** is called by saying **అమ్మా**. What has been added?
options: Nothing: the noun's own final vowel has been lengthened.
drills.explanation: The vocative is the one case that glues nothing on. A noun in -డు may instead shift to -డా, and a noun in -ం is not called at all.

drills.stem: *ఇల్లు* becomes *ఇంటికి* in the dative. What has happened?
options: The suffix is irregular for this noun.
The noun has taken its oblique stem ఇంటి- before the regular suffix.
drills.explanation: -కి is regular; it is the stem that changes. ఇల్లు belongs to the class of six stems whose final syllable becomes -ంటి, beside కన్ను → కంటి and పన్ను → పంటి.

drills.stem: **నీ** ends in ఈ, yet the dative is **నీకు** and not నీకి. What does this show?
options: That the rule of ¶66 has an exception for pronouns with a one-syllable oblique.
That నీ is not really a pronoun.
That నీ has no oblique stem.
drills.explanation: A stem ending in ఇ or ఈ otherwise takes -కి — ఇంటికి, స్త్రీకి. The personal pronouns with a one-syllable oblique are named as the exception, which is why నీకు and మీకు stand beside అతనికి.

drills.stem: Which of these are correctly formed?
drills.explanation: Each pronoun has an oblique stem — నా-, నీ-, మీ- — and the dative is built on that. *నేనుకు* adds the suffix to the nominative, which Telugu never does.

drills.stem: Which statements contrast Telugu with a fusional language such as Lithuanian?
options: A Telugu case suffix keeps one shape across all nouns.
A Telugu suffix can be separated from the stem it is added to.
Telugu fuses case and number into a single ending.
Telugu places its case markers after the noun rather than before.
drills.explanation: Fusing case and number into one indivisible ending is exactly what Lithuanian does and Telugu does not: Telugu adds the plural, then the case, each keeping its own shape.

drills.stem: Which of these nouns have an oblique stem identical with their nominative?
drills.explanation: అమ్మ ends in అ and చెట్టు in a doubled consonant, so both belong to the class that changes nothing. ఇల్లు gives ఇంటి and చేయి gives చేతి, each replacing its final syllable.

drills.stem: **పుస్తకాలలో** — which of these are true of the form?
options: It is built on a plural oblique in -ల.
It carries two pieces after the stem: the plural and then the case.
It uses the second oblique in -ాని-.
Its case suffix is the one meaning *in*.
drills.explanation: పుస్తకాలు gives the oblique పుస్తకాల, and -లో follows it. The second oblique in -ాని- belongs to the singular and appears only before the accusative and the dative, so it has no place here.

drills.stem: Pair each form with the case it stands in.
drills.explanation: ఇంటి is the bare oblique and so the genitive; -కి is the dative, -తో the instrumental, -లో the locative. The three wrong pairings each swap the genitive with a suffixed case, which is the confusion the oblique invites: it looks like a stem waiting for something and is already a case.

drills.stem: Pair each noun with the class its oblique stem belongs to.
drills.explanation: చెట్టు ends in a doubled consonant and changes nothing; ఊరు adds -ి to give ఊరి; కన్ను gives కంటి; రాయి gives రాతి. The distractors swap the two that both end in -ు and the two whose final syllable is replaced — the pairs that look alike from the nominative alone.

drills.stem: How many classes of oblique stem does the singular have?
drills.explanation: Six. The first holds the majority of nouns and changes nothing; the sixth is the class of nouns in -ం, which alone has two obliques.

drills.stem: Which numbered rule states that the oblique stem is the genitive?
drills.explanation: ¶60. ¶61 then divides the obliques into classes and ¶63 gives the plural, but the identification of the oblique with the genitive is what ¶60 states.

drills.stem: **నేను ఇంట్లో ఉన్నాను** — how many of its three words carry a case suffix?
drills.explanation: One: *ఇంట్లో*, the oblique ఇంటి- with -లో. *నేను* is the bare nominative subject, which takes no suffix at all, and the third word is the verb.

drills.stem: Of the seven cases, how many are marked by gluing a suffix onto the stem?
drills.explanation: Four: the dative, the accusative, the instrumental and the locative. The nominative adds nothing, the genitive *is* the oblique stem, and the vocative lengthens the noun's own last vowel. Counting seven reckons every case a suffix; counting five usually forgets that the vocative glues nothing on.

drills.title: పుస్తకం ఎక్కడ?
drills.passage:
రవి: అమ్మా, నా పుస్తకం ఎక్కడ ఉంది?
అమ్మ: ఏ పుస్తకం, నాన్నా? నీ పుస్తకాలు బల్ల మీద ఉన్నాయి.
రవి: బల్ల మీద లేదు. నేను దాన్ని స్నేహితుడికి ఇచ్చాను.
అమ్మ: ఎవరికి?
రవి: రాముడికి. రాముడి ఇల్లు మన ఇంటి దగ్గర ఉంది.
అమ్మ: అయితే రాముడి ఇంటికి వెళ్ళు.
drills.translation:
Ravi: Mother, where is my book?
Mother: Which book, dear? Your books are on the table.
Ravi: It is not on the table. I gave it to a friend.
Mother: To whom?
Ravi: To Ramudu. Ramudu's house is near our house.
Mother: Then go to Ramudu's house.

glossary.నాన్నా: a term a parent uses in addressing a child, of either sex

questions.explanation: *నేను దాన్ని స్నేహితుడికి ఇచ్చాను* … *రాముడికి*. Both carry the dative, which is the case the question itself asks in — ఎవరికి.
*రాముడి ఇల్లు మన ఇంటి దగ్గర ఉంది*. **ఇంటి** here is the bare oblique — a genitive governed by దగ్గర — and not a dative, which would be ఇంటికి.

questions.stem: **రాముడి** appears twice in the passage. Which statements are true of the two occurrences?
options: In *రాముడి ఇల్లు* it is a genitive, and stands alone as one.
In *రాముడి ఇంటికి* it is still a genitive, and the dative is on ఇల్లు.
In *రాముడి ఇంటికి* the dative suffix is on రాముడి.
Both are the oblique stem of రాముడు.
questions.explanation: రాముడి is the oblique of రాముడు in both, and the oblique alone is the genitive. In *రాముడి ఇంటికి* the dative is carried by the second noun — *to Ramudu's house*, not *to Ramudu*.

questions.stem: How many datives does the passage contain?
questions.explanation: Four: *స్నేహితుడికి*, *ఎవరికి*, *రాముడికి* and *ఇంటికి*. *అమ్మా* is a vocative and *రాముడి* a genitive; neither is a dative, though both stand where an English *to* might tempt one to read it.
